section.name: 13. An Introduction to AS Level Organic Chemistry

topic.name: Shapes of Organic Molecules; σ & π Bonds

subtopics.name: Shapes of Organic Molecules; σ & π Bonds

parts.problem_md:
The structure of the amino acid cysteine is shown.

![Structural formula of cysteine showing three carbon atoms: the carboxyl carbon with a C=O double bond, the alpha-carbon bonded to four different groups, and the beta-carbon bonded to the thiol group](assets/001-structural-formula-of-cysteine-showing-three-car.png)

How many carbon atoms in a molecule of cysteine are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- An atom is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised when it is surrounded by three regions of electron density, as a double bond counts as one region
- In cysteine, only the carboxyl carbon (-COOH) is bonded to three groups: a hydroxyl (-OH) group, the adjacent carbon, and a C=O double bond
- The alpha-carbon and beta-carbon each form four σ bonds with no double bonds, so both are sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised

**A** is incorrect as there is one sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon atom in cysteine (the carboxyl carbon). A value of 0 would suggest no carbon atom in the molecule contains a double bond.

**C** is incorrect as only one carbon atom (the carboxyl carbon) is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised. The alpha-carbon has four different single-bond groups attached and is sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised.

**D** is incorrect as only one carbon atom is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised. The alpha-carbon and beta-carbon each form four σ bonds with no double bonds and are therefore sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised.

parts.problem_md:
How many σ bonds and π bonds are present in a double bond?

|   | **σ bonds** | **π bonds** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 0 | 2 |
| **B** | 1 | 1 |
| **C** | 1 | 2 |
| **D** | 2 | 0 |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- A double bond consists of one σ bond, formed by the head-on overlap of atomic orbitals, and one π bond, formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals

**A** is incorrect as a combination of 0 σ bonds and 2 π bonds is not possible. The internuclear axis between two bonded atoms must always be occupied by a σ bond before any π bonds can form.

**C** is incorrect as a combination of 1 σ bond and 2 π bonds is the composition of a triple bond, not a double bond.

**D** is incorrect as a combination of 2 σ bonds and 0 π bonds would suggest a double bond consists of two σ bonds. A double bond always consists of one σ bond and one π bond.

parts.problem_md:
Limonene is found in the peel of citrus fruits.

![Skeletal formula of limonene showing a six-membered carbon ring with an isopropenyl substituent and one endocyclic double bond, giving two C=C double bonds in total](assets/002-skeletal-formula-of-limonene-showing-a-six-membe.png)

How many σ and π bonds are present in this molecule?

|   | **σ** | **π** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | 12 | 2 |
| **B** | 22 | 4 |
| **C** | 24 | 4 |
| **D** | 26 | 2 |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Limonene has the molecular formula C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>16</sub>

![Displayed formula of limonene](assets/003-displayed-formula-of-limonene.png)

- Every covalent bond contains one σ bond

  - The carbon skeleton contains 10 C-C σ bonds and 16 C-H σ bonds
  - This gives 26 σ bonds in total
- Each C=C double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond:

  - Limonene contains two C=C double bonds
  - This gives 2 π bonds

**A** is incorrect as 12 σ bonds accounts only for the visible bonds in the carbon skeleton and does not include the C-H σ bonds to implicit hydrogen atoms. Each CH, CH<sub>2</sub>, or CH<sub>3</sub> group contains additional σ bonds that must be counted.

**B** is incorrect as 4 π bonds would suggest each double bond contains two π bonds. A C=C double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond only, giving 2 π bonds for a molecule with two double bonds.

**C** is incorrect as 24 σ bonds and 4 π bonds reflects an undercount of σ bonds and an overcount of π bonds. Not all C-H σ bonds have been included in the total, and each double bond contributes only one π bond.

parts.problem_md: What is the hybridisation of the carbon atom in methane?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Methane contains four σ bonds between the central carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms
- To form four equivalent bonds, the carbon atom hybridises one s orbital and three p orbitals to give four identical sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals
- Four sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals arrange themselves tetrahedrally to minimise repulsion

**A** is incorrect as sp hybridisation involves mixing one s orbital and one p orbital, producing two hybrid orbitals. This is associated with triple bonds, such as in ethyne.

**B** is incorrect as sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation involves mixing one s orbital and two p orbitals, producing three hybrid orbitals. This is associated with double bonds, such as in ethene.

**D** is incorrect as sp<sup>4</sup> hybridisation is not possible. The p subshell contains only three orbitals (p<sub>x</sub>, p<sub>y</sub>, p<sub>z</sub>), so a maximum of three p orbitals can participate in hybridisation with one s orbital.

parts.problem_md: Which type of bond is formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- A π bond is formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals above and below the internuclear axis

**A** is incorrect as a dative covalent bond is formed when one atom donates both electrons to a shared pair. It is not formed by the sideways overlap of p orbitals.

**B** is incorrect as a hydrogen bond is an intermolecular force of attraction between an electron-deficient hydrogen atom (bonded to N, O, or F) and a lone pair on a neighbouring electronegative atom. It is not formed by orbital overlap.

**D** is incorrect as a σ bond is formed by the head-on (end-to-end) overlap of atomic orbitals along the internuclear axis, not by sideways overlap.

parts.problem_md: What is the bond angle around an sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon atom?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- An sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon atom has three regions of electron density (three σ bonds and no lone pairs)
- Three regions of electron density arrange in a trigonal planar geometry to minimise repulsion
- A trigonal planar geometry gives bond angles of 120°

**A** is incorrect as 104.5° is the bond angle associated with a central atom having two bond pairs and two lone pairs, such as the oxygen atom in water (H<sub>2</sub>O). Carbon does not have two lone pairs in any stable organic molecule.

**B** is incorrect as 109.5° is the bond angle for a perfect tetrahedral geometry, corresponding to sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation with four σ bonds and no lone pairs, such as in methane (CH<sub>4</sub>).

**D** is incorrect as 180° is the bond angle for a linear geometry, corresponding to sp hybridisation with only two regions of electron density, such as in ethyne.

parts.problem_md: What is the minimum number of carbon atoms required to form a chiral acyclic alkane?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- For a carbon atom to be a chiral centre, it must be bonded to four different groups
- In an acyclic alkane, the four substituents are limited to hydrogen atoms and alkyl chains
- The four smallest different substituents are: H (0 additional carbons), methyl (1 carbon), ethyl (2 carbons), and propyl (3 carbons)
- Minimum total: 1 (central chiral carbon) + 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 7 carbon atoms

![Structural formula of 3-methylhexane showing the chiral centre at carbon 3, bonded to four different groups: a hydrogen atom, a methyl group, an ethyl group, and a propyl group](assets/004-structural-formula-of-3-methylhexane-showing-the.jpg)

**A** is incorrect as 6 carbon atoms is not sufficient. After the central chiral carbon, only 5 remain. The three smallest different alkyl groups (methyl, ethyl, propyl) require 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 carbons, but only 5 are available. Any valid distribution of 5 carbons among three groups requires two identical groups, which destroys the chiral centre.

**C** is incorrect as 9 carbon atoms, while sufficient, is not the minimum. The smallest chiral acyclic alkane (3-methylhexane) requires only 7 carbon atoms.

**D** is incorrect as 11 carbon atoms, while sufficient, is not the minimum required to form a chiral acyclic alkane.

parts.problem_md: Which molecule is a straight-chain hydrocarbon?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A straight-chain hydrocarbon consists of a continuous series of carbon atoms without any branches or ring structures
- Propane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) contains a continuous, unbranched chain of three carbon atoms

**A** is incorrect as 2-methylpropane is a branched aliphatic hydrocarbon. The longest continuous chain contains three carbon atoms with a methyl group branching off the central carbon atom.

**B** is incorrect as benzene is an aromatic hydrocarbon. It consists of a planar, cyclic ring of six carbon atoms, not an open chain.

**C** is incorrect as cyclopentane is an alicyclic hydrocarbon. The five carbon atoms form a closed ring rather than an open chain.

parts.problem_md: How many π bonds are present in one molecule of ethene?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- π bonds are formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals
- Ethene contains one carbon-carbon double bond (C=C)
- The C=C double bond consists of one σ bond, formed by head-on orbital overlap, and one π bond, formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals

**A** is incorrect as 0 would suggest ethene contains only single bonds with no π bonds present.

**C** is incorrect as 2 would suggest the C=C double bond consists of two π bonds. A double bond consists of one σ bond and one π bond only.

**D** is incorrect as 3 π bonds would require multiple double or triple bonds, which are not present in ethene.

parts.problem_md:
The diagram shows part of the structure of cysteine, an amino acid, with three bond angles labelled.

![Chemical structure of the amino acid cysteine, with bond angles labelled x, y and z ](assets/005-chemical-structure-of-the-amino-acid-cysteine-wi.png)

What is the correct order of the bond angles *x*, *y* and *z*, from smallest to largest?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Angle *y*:

  - The central carbon atom has four bond pairs and no lone pairs, giving a tetrahedral geometry with a bond angle of 109.5°
- Angle *x*:

  - The nitrogen atom in the amine group has three bond pairs and one lone pair, giving a trigonal pyramidal geometry with a bond angle of 107°
- Angle *z*:

  - The oxygen atom has two bond pairs and two lone pairs, giving a bent geometry with a bond angle of 104.5°
- The correct size order from smallest to largest is *z* (104.5°) < *x* (107°) < *y* (109.5°)
- All three central atoms have a base tetrahedral electron geometry. Lone pairs repel more strongly than bond pairs, compressing the bond angle by approximately 2.5° per lone pair.

**A** is incorrect as *x* < *y* < *z* would place the oxygen atom as having the largest bond angle. Oxygen has two lone pairs, which cause greater repulsion and produce a smaller bond angle than either carbon or nitrogen.

**B** is incorrect as *x* < *z* < *y* incorrectly assigns a smaller angle to oxygen than to nitrogen. Oxygen has two lone pairs (giving 104.5°), which produce a smaller bond angle than the single lone pair on nitrogen (107°).

**D** is incorrect as *z* < *y* < *x* would suggest the nitrogen atom has the largest bond angle. The tetrahedral carbon atom, with no lone pairs, has the largest bond angle of 109.5°.

parts.problem_md:
Methyl isocyanate, CH<sub>3</sub>NCO, is a toxic liquid which is used in the production of adhesives.

The sequence of atoms in a methyl isocyanate molecule is H<sub>3</sub>C—N=C=O.

What is the approximate angle between the bonds formed by the N atom?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- From the sequence H<sub>3</sub>C—N=C=O, the nitrogen atom forms a single bond with the methyl group and a double bond with the isocyanate carbon
- Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons; after forming these bonds, one lone pair remains
- The nitrogen atom therefore has three regions of electron density: two bonding regions and one lone pair

![Dot-and-cross diagram of the nitrogen atom in methyl isocyanate showing three regions of electron density in a trigonal planar arrangement](assets/006-dot-and-cross-diagram-of-the-nitrogen-atom-in-me.jpg)

- Three regions of electron density arrange in a trigonal planar geometry, giving an approximate bond angle of 120° (slightly less than 120° due to the greater repulsion from the lone pair)

**A** is incorrect as 107° is the bond angle in ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>), where nitrogen has three bonding pairs and one lone pair giving a tetrahedral electron geometry. In methyl isocyanate, the nitrogen has three regions of electron density, not four.

**B** is incorrect as 109.5° is the bond angle for a perfect tetrahedral geometry with four bonding pairs and no lone pairs. The nitrogen in methyl isocyanate has three regions of electron density, giving a trigonal planar geometry.

**D** is incorrect as 180° is the bond angle for a linear geometry with only two regions of electron density. The carbon atom in the isocyanate group (—N=C=O) has a 180° bond angle, not the nitrogen atom.

parts.problem_md:
The structure of ibuprofen is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Skeletal structure of ibuprofen showing benzene ring, carboxylic acid, and isobutyl chain](assets/007-skeletal-structure-of-ibuprofen-showing-benzene-.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State the number of pi (π) bonds and the number of chiral centres in a molecule of ibuprofen.

number of π bonds ..............................

number of chiral centres ..............................
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of pi (π) bonds and chiral centres in ibuprofen is:
> 
> - π bonds = 4 **[1 mark]**
> - chiral centres = 1 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To count π bonds: each double bond contains one π bond. In ibuprofen, the benzene ring has 3 (shown in the Kekulé structure) and the carboxylic acid has 1 C=O, giving 4 π bonds total.
> 
> A chiral centre is a carbon atom bonded to four different groups. In ibuprofen, the carbon bearing the methyl group, the carboxylic acid group, the isobutyl chain, and a hydrogen atom is the only chiral centre (1 total).

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The structure of ibuprofen is shown in Fig. 1.1.

Fig. 1.1

State the number of sp<sup>2</sup> and sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon atoms in a molecule of ibuprofen.

sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon atoms ..............................

sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon atoms ..............................
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of sp<sup>2</sup> and sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon atoms in ibuprofen is:
> 
> - sp<sup>2</sup> = 7 **[1 mark]**
> - sp<sup>3</sup> = 6 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each carbon with a tetrahedral arrangement of bonds (four single bonds only) is sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised. Each carbon in the benzene ring and the carbonyl carbon are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised.
> 
> ![Diagram of a ibuprofen molecule showing sp2 (green) and sp3 (blue) hybridised carbon atoms, with labelled CH3 side groups and a carboxylic acid](assets/008-diagram-of-a-ibuprofen-molecule-showing-sp2-gree.png)
> 
> When counting, look for double bonds and aromatic ring carbons first, these are sp<sup>2</sup>. Any carbon with only single bonds is sp<sup>3</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The structure of ibuprofen is shown in Fig. 1.1.

Describe and explain the shape of the benzene ring in ibuprofen.

In your answer, include:

- the bond angle between carbon atoms
- the hybridisation of the carbon atoms
- how orbital overlap forms σ and π bonds between the carbon atoms
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The shape of the benzene ring in ibuprofen is:
> 
> - Bond angle between carbon atoms is 120° **[1 mark]**
> - All carbon atoms in the ring are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals overlap head-on to form σ bonds between adjacent carbons; the unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to form a delocalised π system above and below the ring **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> All carbons in the benzene ring are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised, giving a trigonal planar arrangement around each carbon with bond angles of 120°. This forces all six carbons into the same plane, making the ring planar.
> 
> The sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals form sigma bonds between adjacent carbon atoms (head-on overlap). Each carbon also has one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the ring; these overlap sideways with neighbouring p orbitals to form a delocalised π system above and below the plane of the ring.

parts.problem_md:
Gasoline is a mixture of hydrocarbons. Compound **X** is a component of gasoline. The displayed formula of compound **X** is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Displayed formula of 2,2-dimethylpentane, a branched alkane component of gasoline](assets/009-displayed-formula-of-2-2-dimethylpentane-a-branc.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

i) State the systematic name of compound **X**.

[1]

ii) State the general formula for the homologous series to which compound **X** belongs.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The systematic name of compound **X** is:
> 
> - 2,2-dimethylpentane **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The general formula for the homologous series to which compound **X** belongs is:
> 
> - C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To name compound **X**:
> 
> - The longest carbon chain is 5 carbons, so the name is pentane-based
> - There are only C–C single bonds, so it is an alkane
> - There are two methyl groups on carbon-2, giving the prefix 2,2-dimethyl
> - Full systematic name: 2,2-dimethylpentane
> 
> The compound belongs to the alkane homologous series, which has the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>.

ii) Draw the skeletal formulae of the **four** monochlorinated isomers formed when compound **X** reacts with chlorine.

iii) State the type of structural isomerism shown by the isomers in **(ii)**.

parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The mechanism for this reaction is:
> 
> - Free radical substitution **[1 mark]**

ii) The skeletal formulae of the four monochlorinated isomers of compound **X** are:

2,2-dimethyl-5-chloropentane

![Skeletal formula of monochlorinated isomer with chlorine at the 2,2-dimethyl position](assets/010-skeletal-formula-of-monochlorinated-isomer-with-.png)

**[1 mark]**

2,2-dimethyl-4-chloropentane

![Skeletal formula of monochlorinated isomer with chlorine at carbon-3](assets/011-skeletal-formula-of-monochlorinated-isomer-with-.png)

**[1 mark]**

2,2-dimethyl-3-chloropentane

![Skeletal formula of monochlorinated isomer with chlorine at carbon-4](assets/012-skeletal-formula-of-monochlorinated-isomer-with-.png)

**[1 mark]**

Plus, any **one** of the following 2,2-dimethyl-1-chloropentane structures:

![Skeletal formula of monochlorinated isomer with chlorine at the terminal carbon, representation A](assets/013-skeletal-formula-of-monochlorinated-isomer-with-.png)

**OR**

![Skeletal formula of monochlorinated isomer with chlorine at the terminal carbon, representation B](assets/014-skeletal-formula-of-monochlorinated-isomer-with-.png)

**OR**

![Skeletal formula of monochlorinated isomer with chlorine at the terminal carbon, representation C](assets/015-skeletal-formula-of-monochlorinated-isomer-with-.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the correct structure of 2,2-dimethyl-5-chloropentane
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure of 2,2-dimethyl-4-chloropentane
> 
> 1 mark for the correct structure of 2,2-dimethyl-3-chloropentane
> 
> 1 mark for one of the correct structures of 2,2-dimethyl-1-chloropentane
> 
> The three structures shown as alternatives for the fourth mark are all representations of the same compound; any one is accepted.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) The type of structural isomerism shown by the isomers in (ii) is:
> 
> - Positional isomerism **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part (i): alkanes are relatively unreactive. The combination of a halogen and UV light is the characteristic condition for free radical substitution.
> 
> For part (ii): compound X is being monochlorinated, meaning one hydrogen atom is replaced by one chlorine atom. Draw a skeletal formula for each unique position where chlorine can be substituted. The first three isomers in the mark scheme are all distinct; the last three structures are different representations of the same compound.
> 
> For part (iii): the isomers have the same molecular formula and the same carbon chain, differing only in the position of the chlorine atom. This is positional isomerism.

parts.problem_md:
Fig. 2.2 shows the mechanism for the reaction of aqueous sodium hydroxide with 1-bromopropane.

![SN2 mechanism showing hydroxide ion attacking 1-bromopropane to form compound X with bromide leaving](assets/016-sn2-mechanism-showing-hydroxide-ion-attacking-1-.png)

**Fig. 2.2**

i) State the role of the aqueous hydroxide ion in this reaction.

[1]

ii) State the systematic name of compound **X**.

[1]

iii) Under different reaction conditions, 1-bromopropane reacts with hydroxide ions to form propene.

State the conditions required for this reaction and name the mechanism.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The role of the aqueous hydroxide ion in this reaction is:
> 
> - Nucleophile **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The systematic name of compound **X** is:
> 
> - Propan-1-ol **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The conditions and mechanism for this alternative reaction are:
> 
> - Conditions: Heat / warm
> **AND**
> Alcoholic / ethanolic (sodium) hydroxide **[1 mark]**
> - Mechanism: Elimination **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You should know both reactions of a halogenoalkane with hydroxide ions:
> 
> - Aqueous NaOH: nucleophilic substitution, forming an alcohol
> - Alcoholic / ethanolic NaOH with heat: elimination, forming an alkene and water
> 
> Both conditions require the hydroxide ion, but its role changes depending on whether aqueous or alcoholic solvent is used.

parts.problem_md:
Pentanal reacts with HCN in the presence of NaCN to form 2-hydroxyhexanenitrile as shown in Fig. 2.3.

![Reaction scheme showing pentanal reacting with HCN and NaCN to form 2-hydroxyhexanenitrile, with the carbonyl carbon highlighted](assets/017-reaction-scheme-showing-pentanal-reacting-with-h.png)

**Fig. 2.3**

i) By reference to hybridisation and orbital overlap, explain why the carbonyl carbon in pentanal is trigonal planar.

[3]

ii) State the shape and bond angle around carbon-2 in 2-hydroxyhexanenitrile.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) By reference to hybridisation and orbital overlap, the carbonyl carbon in pentanal is trigonal planar because:
> 
> - The carbonyl carbon is sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised / the carbonyl bond contains one σ bond **[1 mark]**
> - The unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways to form a π bond **[1 mark]**
> - The bonding pairs of electrons are in the same plane
> **AND**
> This causes repulsion, giving a trigonal planar shape **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The shape and bond angle around carbon-2 in 2-hydroxyhexanenitrile are:
> 
> - Tetrahedral
> **AND**
> 109.5° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Any time there is planarity within a molecule, hybridisation is involved. State the hybridisation (sp<sup>2</sup>) and explain how the σ and π bonds are formed from orbital overlap.
> 
> For part (ii): carbon-2 in the product has reacted and now has four different groups attached, so it adopts a tetrahedral geometry with bond angles of 109.5°. A common error is to give the answer as linear and 180°, which describes the nitrile carbon at the end of the chain (from the HCN), not carbon-2.

parts.problem_md: By reference to the hybridisation of the carbon atoms and orbital overlap, describe how the σ and π bonds are formed in the triple bond of propyne.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The σ and π bonds in the triple bond of propyne are formed as follows:
> 
> - The carbon atoms forming the triple bond are sp hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - The σ bond is formed from the head-on overlap of sp orbitals (from each carbon atom) **[1 mark]**
> - Two π bonds are formed from the sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals (on each carbon atom) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A triple bond consists of one σ bond and two π bonds. To form a triple bond, the two carbon atoms must be sp hybridised.
> 
> The σ bond forms from the head-on (direct) overlap of one sp orbital from each carbon atom. The two π bonds are formed from the sideways overlap of the two unhybridised p orbitals on each carbon.

parts.problem_md:
The structure of an organic molecule is shown in Fig. 1.1.

![Organic molecule containing sigma and pi bonds](assets/018-organic-molecule-containing-sigma-and-pi-bonds.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

State the number of carbon atoms that are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised in this molecule.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The number of sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon atoms in this molecule is:
> 
> - Six / 6 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Only carbon atoms involved in double bonds are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised. When counting, it is easy to accidentally count the number of double bonds rather than the number of sp<sup>2</sup> carbons. Remember that each double bond involves two carbon atoms, both of which are sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised.

parts.problem_md:
Complete Table 1.1 to state the hybridisation of the nitrogen atom in each species.

**Table 1.1**

|   | ** NF**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**+**</sup> | **N**<sub>**2**</sub>**H**<sub>**2**</sub> | **N**<sub>**2**</sub>**H**<sub>**4**</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|
| hybridisation |   |   |   |
parts.solution_md:
The completed Table 1.1 is:

|   | ** NF**<sub>**4**</sub><sup>**+**</sup> | **N**<sub>**2**</sub>**H**<sub>**2**</sub> | **N**<sub>**2**</sub>**H**<sub>**4**</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|
| hybridisation | **Final answer:** **sp**<sup>**3**</sup> | **Final answer:** **sp**<sup>**2**</sup> | **Final answer:** **sp**<sup>**3**</sup> |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation for NF<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation for N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>
> 
> 1 mark for sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation for N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use the number of electron domains around each nitrogen atom to determine the hybridisation:
> 
> - 4 electron domains = sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation (e.g. NF<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> has 4 bond pairs; N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair)
> - 3 electron domains = sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation (e.g. N<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> has 2 bond pairs and 1 lone pair)
> - 2 electron domains = sp hybridisation
> 
> Drawing the Lewis structure for each species first is a reliable way to count electron domains without making errors.

parts.problem_md:
The carbon chain of an aliphatic organic molecule can be described as straight-chained.

State two other terms used to describe the arrangement of carbon atoms in an aliphatic organic molecule.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**

parts.problem_md:
Complete Table 1.1 to state the number of σ and π bonds in each type of hybridised bond.

**Table 1.1**

| hybridisation | number of σ bonds | number of π bonds |
|---|---|---|
| sp<sup>3</sup> |   |   |
| sp<sup>2</sup> |   |   |
| sp |   |   |
parts.solution_md:
The completed Table 1.1 is:

| hybridisation | number of σ bonds | number of π bonds |
|---|---|---|
| sp<sup>3</sup> | **Final answer:** **4** | **Final answer:** **0** |
| sp<sup>2</sup> | **Final answer:** **3** | **Final answer:** **1** |
| sp | **Final answer:** **2** | **Final answer:** **2** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for sp<sup>3</sup>: 4 σ bonds and 0 π bonds
> 
> 1 mark for sp<sup>2</sup>: 3 σ bonds and 1 π bond
> 
> 1 mark for sp: 2 σ bonds and 2 π bonds

> **[exam-tip]**
> Each sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon forms 4 sigma bonds (from the 4 sp<sup>3</sup> orbitals overlapping head-on) and no pi bonds, because all valence orbitals are involved in hybridisation.
> 
> An sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon forms 3 sigma bonds and 1 pi bond: the 3 sp<sup>2</sup> orbitals each form a sigma bond, and the remaining unhybridised p orbital overlaps sideways with an adjacent p orbital to form 1 pi bond.
> 
> An sp hybridised carbon forms 2 sigma bonds and 2 pi bonds: the 2 sp orbitals each form a sigma bond, and the 2 unhybridised p orbitals each overlap sideways to form 2 pi bonds.

> 
> Note that not all of these molecules are planar: water is non-linear (V-shaped), not flat.

parts.problem_md: Explain why the ring of carbon atoms in cyclohexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, is non-planar. In your answer, refer to the hybridisation of the carbon atoms and the C–C–C bond angles.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Cyclohexane has a non-planar ring of carbon atoms because:
> 
> - The carbon atoms are sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised **[1 mark]**
> - Each carbon has a tetrahedral arrangement of bonds
> **AND**
> The C–C–C bond angles are 109.5° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Hybridisation determines the geometry around each atom:
> 
> - sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised carbon ↔ tetrahedral geometry ↔ bond angles of 109.5°
> - sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised carbon ↔ trigonal planar geometry ↔ bond angles of 120°
> - sp hybridised carbon ↔ linear geometry ↔ bond angles of 180°
> 
> In cyclohexane, the 109.5° tetrahedral bond angles prevent the ring from being flat:
> 
> ![Skeletal formula of cyclohexane showing six linked carbon atoms, each bonded to hydrogen atoms, illustrating a non-planar branched hydrocarbon structure](assets/020-skeletal-formula-of-cyclohexane-showing-six-link.png)
> 
> A flat ring would require 120° bond angles, which would require sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation and double bonds. The puckered shape allows each carbon to maintain its preferred tetrahedral geometry.

parts.solution_md:
The completed Table 3.1 is:

| atom | hybridisation | approximate bond angle / ° |
|---|---|---|
| carbon | **Final answer:** **sp**<sup>**2**</sup> | **Final answer:** **120** |
| nitrogen | **Final answer:** **sp**<sup>**3**</sup> | **Final answer:** **109.5** |

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation of carbon
> 
> 1 mark for approximate bond angle of 120° for carbon
> 
> 1 mark for sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation of each nitrogen atom
> 
> 1 mark for approximate bond angle of 109.5° for each nitrogen atom

> **[exam-tip]**
> Use the number of electron domains around each atom:
> 
> - Carbon has 3 electron domains (one C=O double bond counts as one domain, plus two N–C single bonds) → sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised, bond angle ~120°
> - Each nitrogen has 4 electron domains (two N–H bonds, one N–C bond, one lone pair) → sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised, bond angle ~109.5°
> 
> Drawing the Lewis structure first makes it straightforward to count electron domains.

parts.problem_md:
State the hybridisation of the carbon atom in methane, CH<sub>4</sub>. Name the shape of the molecule and explain why it has this shape.

hybridisation:

shape:

explanation:
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The hybridisation and shape of the carbon atom in methane are:
> 
> - Hybridisation: sp<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Shape: tetrahedral **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - 4 bonding pairs of electrons (4 electron domains) around the central carbon **[1 mark]**
> - The electron pairs repel equally to maximise separation, giving bond angles of 109.5° **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The carbon atom in methane is sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised because it forms four identical single bonds. The four sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals repel each other equally, adopting a tetrahedral geometry to maximise separation between bonding pairs.
> 
> The bond angle in methane is 109.5°, the ideal tetrahedral angle.

parts.problem_md:
A molecule of ethanol is shown in Fig. 3.2.

![Displayed formula of ethanol with one carbon atom labelled](assets/022-displayed-formula-of-ethanol-with-one-carbon-ato.png)

**Fig. 3.2**

State the hybridisation of the carbon atom marked in Fig. 3.2.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The hybridisation of the carbon atom marked in Fig. 3.2 is:
> 
> - sp<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both carbon atoms in ethanol form only single bonds and have no lone pairs, giving 4 electron domains around each carbon. This means both are sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised, with a tetrahedral arrangement and bond angles of approximately 109.5°. The oxygen atom is also sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised.
